newsitem.title: TURKEY: Rival Kurds said to clash near Iranian border.
newsitem.headline: Rival Kurds said to clash near Iranian border.

text.p: Separatist rebels of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) have attacked their Iraqi Kurdish rivals, now allied with Turkey, in fierce fighting near Iraq's border with Iran, reports from the region said on Tuesday.
Iraqi opposition sources, citing satellite telephone links with the area, said about 2,000 guerrillas of the PKK, backed by other local forces, had clashed with the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP).
The KDP is backing the latest Turkish military bid to drive the PKK from northern Iraq.
"There is a big battle near Haji Homaran, but so far we have no word on casualties," said a spokesman for the opposition Iraqi National Congress, based in London.
The entire region remains closed to journalists and independent confirmation was impossible.

The fighting, which so far did not involve the Turkish forces allied with the KDP, was heaviest around Haji Homaran, where the colonial-era Hamilton Road crosses from Iraq into Iran, the spokesman said.

He said the PKK, battling for self-rule in neighbouring sourthern Turkey, had been joined by the Kurdish Hizbollah, the Kurdistan Conservative Party and the Kurdistan Social Democratic Party -- all believed to have close ties to Iran.
The PKK and the Conservative Party signed a protocol last week, deciding on a joint struggle against the Turkish army and the KDP, the Kurdish language Med TV said.
"The KDP is a hostile force that has betrayed all national values and that serves the colonialists," Med TV quoted the protocol as saying.
Meanwhile, the KDP, the main power in northern Iraq, has sent two corps of 2,000 peshmerga guerrillas each to the area.
The INC said between 700 to 1,000 PKK guerrillas have crossed into the Hakurk region of northern Iraq from neighbouring Iran armed with Soviet-designed Grad multiple missile launchers.

Turkish forces poured into northern Iraq on May 14 as part of a coordinated strike with the KDP against rebel PKK bases used to hit targets across the border in Turkey. Each side claims to have inflicted heavy losses on the other.
The incursion, involving thousands of troops backed by air power, has sparked widespread criticism across the Middle East.

Turkey has struck back blaming Iran, Syria and other countries for providing the PKK with sophisticated weaponry, including the shoulder-fired SA-7 missiles used to shoot down two Turkish helicopters.
Iran, which denies the charges, sent its deputy foreign minister, Alaeddin Boroujerdi, with a message for Turkish President Suleyman Demirel
The two are scheduled to meet later on Tuesday.
